Vertigo business cards

April Greiman’s business cards for the Los Angeles shop Vertigo: a letterspaced wordmark on a tilted bar, with stripes, dots, and diagonal lines that change from card to card.

Source
People’s Graphic Design Archive: Vertigo business cards
Creator
April Greiman
Made
1980 (People’s Graphic Design Archive)
Style
New Wave typography (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Kinetic, playful, layered, experimental
Evidence
Inspected the People’s Graphic Design Archive image (901 × 1500), a black-and-white photograph of four cards, probably reproduced from a publication; the owner of the physical cards is not stated. Not stored. Colours are not visible.

Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The People’s Graphic Design Archive credits the cards to April Greiman for the client Vertigo/Lynda Weinman, printed by McCoy Printing, and dates them 1980. People’s Graphic Design Archive.

Observed

  • Each card carries the wordmark “Vertigo” on a tilted rectangular bar. The V is a solid black triangle, a slash replaces the i, and a black dot follows the o.
  • The letters of the wordmark are spaced wide apart.
  • The four cards have different grounds: black vertical stripes that extend past the card edge, a dark card with round holes or dots, a light card with thin diagonal lines and circles, and a card with a pattern of rounded squares.
  • Addresses are set in small bold grotesque, some lines tilted or letterspaced (“L o s A n g e l e s”).
  • Small words such as “gifts”, “paper”, and “fashion acces.” run along diagonal lines.

Why it belongs

The cards turn a small identity into a system of variations: one tilted, spaced wordmark stays fixed while the surfaces change. This is the style’s move from the poster to everyday print.

Borrow

Put a letterspaced wordmark on a slightly tilted solid bar.

Replace one letter with a geometric mark (a triangle, a slash, a dot).

Keep the mark fixed and change the surface pattern across a set of cards.
